issues.legal_issue: A law placed in the constitutional schedule before the relevant cutoff is protected from challenge for violating fundamental rights.
material_facts: The challenged 1955 land-reform law and the 1972 amendments had been placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973.
The petitioners conceded that the constitutional challenge to those laws was concluded by the Court's decision in Waman Rao.
issues.conclusion: The 1955 Act and the 1972 amendments were immune from challenge on the ground that they violated Part III of the Constitution.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protects laws included in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973, from challenges based on inconsistency with or abridgment of Part III rights. The Court applied Waman Rao v. Union of India.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_fundamental_rights_val: A person brought a constitutional proceeding challenging a law on the ground that it violates fundamental rights.
predicates.law_was_scheduled_before_cutoff: The challenged law had been included in the protected constitutional schedule before the relevant cutoff.

issues.definition: When a fundamental-rights challenge concerns a law included in the protected schedule before the cutoff, the law is immune from that challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Enumerated statutory grounds for resuming land cannot be expanded to include a bargadar's voluntary surrender or abandonment when that circumstance is not covered by those grounds.
material_facts: The law listed specific circumstances in which a tenant could terminate a bargadar's cultivation and resume the land for personal cultivation.
A bargadar's voluntary surrender or abandonment was not among those circumstances.
The respondents asked the Court to interpret one listed ground as allowing resumption after voluntary surrender or abandonment.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected that interpretation because it would add a circumstance not contained in the statutory grounds for resumption.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the ordinary canons of interpretation: a court cannot distort clear statutory language or introduce into a provision a ground that the provision does not contain. It held that the listed grounds in section 17(1) did not mention or contemplate voluntary surrender or abandonment.

predicates.writ_challenge_to_tenancy_rules: A person brought a constitutional proceeding concerning statutory rules governing a tenant's land cultivated by a sharecropper.
predicates.bargadar_voluntarily_surrendered_or_aban: The sharecropper voluntarily gave up or abandoned cultivation of the land.
predicates.enumerated_resumption_grounds_do_not_cov: The statute's stated grounds for resuming personal cultivation did not include the sharecropper's voluntary surrender or abandonment.

issues.definition: When a sharecropper voluntarily gives up or abandons cultivation and the statutory grounds do not cover that event, a court cannot add it to those grounds by interpretation.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot invalidate protected land-reform restrictions merely because they are harsh or burden a cultivator's rights when the restrictions are part of a law protected from fundamental-rights challenge.
material_facts: The challenged provisions prevented a tenant from resuming personal cultivation after a bargadar voluntarily surrendered or abandoned the land, and instead required cultivation by another person with official permission.
The Court considered the provisions harsh and said they bordered on arbitrariness and seriously curbed the cultivator's occupational rights.
The provisions were part of the 1972 amendment, which had been placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973.
issues.conclusion: The Court could not strike down the provisions because they were protected from fundamental-rights challenge; it left it to the legislature to soften their rigour.
issues.legal_principle: Article 31B protects qualifying Ninth Schedule laws from challenges based on Part III. Under Waman Rao v. Union of India, laws placed in the Ninth Schedule before April 24, 1973, receive that protection. The Court also observed that legislative relief could address the provisions' harshness.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_land_cultiva: A person brought a constitutional proceeding challenging restrictions on a landholder's ability to cultivate land personally.
predicates.restrictions_bar_personal_resumption_aft: The restrictions prevent a landholder from resuming personal cultivation after a sharecropper voluntarily gives up or abandons cultivation.
predicates.law_was_scheduled_before_cutoff: The law containing the restrictions had been included in the protected constitutional schedule before the relevant cutoff.

issues.definition: When a protected law bars personal resumption after voluntary surrender, the court cannot strike down that restriction on fundamental-rights grounds.

issues.legal_issue: A requirement that a landholder or a member of the landholder's family reside in the locality for most of the year, where the land is held for personal cultivation and agriculture is the principal source of income, is a reasonable restriction on residence and occupational rights.
material_facts: The challenged condition required the landholder or a family member to reside in the locality where the land was situated for the greater part of the year.
The condition also required the principal source of income to come from the land.
The tenant was not barred from pursuing another occupation, and the tenant could reside elsewhere for part of the year.
The family definition permitted a family member, rather than the tenant personally, to satisfy the residence condition.
The Court found the condition connected to personal cultivation, the prevention of absentee landholding, and the public interest in agrarian reform.
issues.conclusion: The residence and income conditions were reasonable restrictions and did not violate the rights to reside anywhere in India or to carry on an occupation.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 19(1)(e) and 19(1)(g) are subject to reasonable restrictions under Articles 19(4) and 19(5). The Court applied the contextual reasonableness approach in State of Madras v. V.G. Row, considering the nature of the rights, the purpose of the restriction, its extent, and the conditions addressed. It held that the restriction was partial, served agrarian reform and public interest, and was not disproportionate.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_residence_an: A person brought a constitutional proceeding challenging a condition affecting where a landholder may reside and what occupation the landholder may pursue.
predicates.land_is_reserved_for_personal_cultivatio: The land is made available to a holder on the basis that it will be personally cultivated.
predicates.agriculture_is_principal_income_source: The condition is limited to a holder whose principal source of income comes from the land.
predicates.tenant_or_family_member_must_reside_loca: The condition requires the holder or a member of the holder's family to reside in the locality for most of the year.
predicates.condition_allows_other_occupation_and_pa: The condition does not prohibit other occupations or require residence in the locality throughout the entire year.

issues.definition: When land is reserved for personal cultivation by a holder principally supported by agriculture, a partial residence condition allowing other work and some absence is reasonable.

issues.legal_issue: A residence condition does not discriminate contrary to equality where it applies equally to all persons governed by it and bears a connection to the purpose of personal cultivation.
material_facts: The condition required a landholder or a family member to reside locally for most of the year in connection with the cultivation of the land.
The condition applied equally to all tenants governed by it.
The Court found that the condition was directed to ensuring cultivation and increasing the land's produce.
issues.conclusion: The condition did not violate Article 14 because it applied equally to all tenants governed by it and was not arbitrary.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 does not invalidate a condition for discrimination where the condition operates equally on all persons within its scope and is connected to its stated purpose. The Court also considered whether the condition was arbitrary and found no element of arbitrariness.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_on_equality_gro: A person brought a constitutional proceeding alleging that a legal condition discriminates among those it governs.
predicates.residence_condition_applies_equally_to_c: The same residence condition applies to all holders within its scope.
predicates.condition_is_connected_to_personal_culti: The residence condition is directed to ensuring that the land is cultivated personally and productively.

issues.definition: When a residence condition applies equally to covered holders and is connected to personal cultivation, it does not violate equality.
